primary_claim: Contextual Constitutional AI, which selects critique/revision principles based on prompt-response context rather than randomly, did not outperform standard (pure) or mixed CAI on either helpfulness (MT-Bench LLM-judge) or harmlessness (manual inspection against DAN jailbreak prompts) in a small-scale Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 DPO fine-tuning experiment -- it was markedly more vulnerable to DAN jailbreak prompts (4-5/10 harmless) than pure/mixed CAI (10/10), while mixed CAI achieved the best balance of helpfulness and harmlessness among the three CAI variants.

effect.metric: MT-Bench LLM-judge mean helpfulness score (1-10) / fraction of DAN-prompt responses avoided as harmful
effect.value: helpfulness (SFT+DPO): mixed CAI 6.15 > pure CAI 6.01 > contextual CAI 5.81 (baseline instruct 6.62); DAN-prompt harmlessness: contextual CAI 4/10 vs pure/mixed CAI 10/10

contradicts_or_qualifies: qualifies the author's own hypothesis that contextual CAI (context-based principle selection) would yield higher-quality feedback and better models than randomized CAI -- contextual CAI instead underperformed both pure and mixed CAI on helpfulness and was markedly more vulnerable to DAN jailbreak prompts
stated_future_work: increasing the number of red-teamed prompts substantially to see how contextual CAI performs compared to other methods
varying size and proportion of helpful/harmlessness datasets for finetuning
